title: Re-delivering an 'assigned' task never uses up an attempt, so a task the node cannot start is handed back forever and blocks that node
scenario: A token holder sends POST /tasks {"kind":"generate","payload":{"prompt":"hi","temperature":NaN}}. Python's json.loads accepts NaN, and create_task's json.dumps size check allows it. The iPad claims the task, and the response contains the literal NaN. Swift's JSONDecoder rejects it, so NodeService.execute logs 'Undecodable task' and returns without calling /complete (NodeService.swift:174 on origin/ios-node). The task stays 'assigned' to that iPad. The new next_task code returns any 'assigned' task owned by the polling node before it claims new work, and it does not increment attempts. Every poll therefore returns the same undecodable task. The node never gets other work, the task never reaches max_attempts or 'lost', and sweep() never requeues it because the node is online. Any federated round pinned to that node stalls until its deadline. Before this PR the task was orphaned but the node kept serving other work; now the node is blocked until someone manually cancels the task.
evidence: Ran in a temp copy of origin/fix-worker: after creating the NaN task and claiming it once, three more GET /nodes/ipad-aaaa/next?wait=0 calls each returned the same task with 'NaN' in the body and attempts still 1. fleet.py:231-233: `if t.meta["status"] == "assigned": self.nodes[node_id]["last_seen"] = now(); return self.public(t)`. No attempts or redelivery counter is incremented.
fix: Count redeliveries. Either increment attempts or keep a separate `deliveries` counter on each redelivery, and once it exceeds max_attempts call _requeue_or_lose or _finish(..., 'lost'). Also reject non-finite numbers on task creation: use json.dumps(payload, allow_nan=False) in create_task, and allow_nan=False or parse_constant in _body, so no meta can contain NaN or Infinity.
notes:
UPHELD(high): I could not refute this. I checked the code at origin/fix-worker and origin/ios-node, and every step of the claimed path holds.
(1) Python accepts and stores NaN: jobworker.py _body calls json.loads(raw) with default settings, so NaN is accepted. create_task (fleet.py:178) checks size with a plain json.dumps, which allows NaN, so the payload is stored and served back as a literal NaN token.
(2) The iPad cannot decode it: FleetClient.nextTask (FleetClient.swift:126) already decodes the whole response with Self.decoder. Foundation's JSONDecoder rejects a bare NaN token, so the failure actually happens there, one step before the claimed NodeService.swift:174. nextTask throws, the run loop's catch sets lastError and backs off up to 60 s, then polls again. /complete is never called on either path.
(3) The server re-delivers the same task forever: fleet.py:231-233 in next_task returns any task with status 'assigned' and assigned_to == node_id before calling _claim. That branch does not increment attempts or check max_attempts. attempts only goes up in the fresh-claim path (around line 247). The node keeps heartbeating and polling, so it stays online and sweep() never calls _requeue_or_lose. The task stays 'assigned', the node never claims other work, and a federated round pinned to that node stalls until its deadline.
The trigger needs a bearer token holder, but any authorized client can cause it by mistake. Any other server/client decoding mismatch, not just NaN, triggers the same lockup. Before this PR the poll path went straight to _claim, so the node kept taking other work. The regression is real and medium severity is fair. | fix: In fleet.py next_task, count each re-delivery of an 'assigned' task, either as a per-task 'deliveries' counter or by incrementing attempts. Once the count reaches max_attempts, call _requeue_or_lose(t, 'undeliverable/never started') or _finish(t, 'lost', ...), then continue on to _claim. Also reject non-finite numbers at the boundary: in _body, call json.loads(raw, parse_constant=lambda c: (_ for _ in ()).throw(ValueError('non-finite number'))). In create_task, call json.dumps(payload, allow_nan=False). That way no task meta can contain NaN or Infinity. Optionally, on the iPad side, when a task cannot be decoded, extract the task id with a lenient parse and POST /complete with status=failed.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute this. On origin/fix-worker, worker/fleet.py next_task loops over the tasks owned by the polling node first. If one has status "assigned", it updates last_seen and returns self.public(t) right away. That path never touches attempts, never calls _requeue_or_lose, and never passes through max_attempts. sweep() requeues assigned or running tasks only when the owning node is offline. A node that keeps polling stays online, so nothing ever frees the task.

Nothing upstream blocks the bad input either. create_task calls json.dumps(payload) with the default allow_nan=True, and jobworker._body calls json.loads(raw) with no parse_constant, so a NaN or Infinity in the payload is stored. public() then serializes it back out as the literal NaN, which is invalid JSON. Apple's JSONSerialization and JSONDecoder reject that literal unless JSON5 is enabled.

On origin/ios-node, in ios/AgentConsole/Node/NodeService.swift, execute() catches the decode error at line 174, sets lastError, and returns without calling /complete or posting events. Because no events are posted, the task never moves to "running", so the abandoned-task requeue branch never fires. runLoop then calls nextTask again at once and gets the same task back immediately without waiting. The iPad spins in a hot loop, never gets other work, and the task never reaches "lost".

Other inputs trigger the same failure: any decodeTask failure, such as an id or kind of the wrong type, or a payload shape an older app build cannot parse. The poster's temp-copy repro matches the code: the same task was returned on every poll and attempts stayed at 1. Severity medium is fair, since it needs a token holder to submit the bad task, but it blocks the node and burns its battery. | fix: In next_task, when re-delivering an "assigned" task, increment a deliveries counter (or attempts). Once it exceeds max_attempts, call _finish(t, "failed"/"lost", reason="node could not start task") instead of returning it. As a defensive measure, validate at creation with json.dumps(payload, allow_nan=False) in create_task, and use json.loads(raw, parse_constant=_reject) in _body. Optionally, NodeService.execute should report a failed /complete when decoding fails but the id is recoverable.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute the claim. Each step of the scenario checks out against the code.

1. Task creation. In origin/fix-worker worker/fleet.py:173-196, create_task checks only kind, that payload is a dict, `len(json.dumps(payload))` (allow_nan defaults to True) and that prompt is a string. A NaN temperature passes all of these, and the body is parsed by json.loads, which accepts the NaN literal.

2. Claim. At fleet.py:246-249 the first claim sets attempts to 1 and the status to 'assigned'. The response is serialized with the default json.dumps, so it contains the literal NaN.

3. iPad side. In origin/ios-node ios/AgentConsole/Node/NodeService.swift:169-176, if decodeTask throws, the code sets lastError = "Undecodable task" and returns. It never calls /complete or /events, so the task stays 'assigned' to that node. Swift's default JSONDecoder rejects NaN.

4. Re-delivery (new in this PR; the diff shows lines 140-145 added). On every later poll, next_task at fleet.py:228-233 finds the 'assigned' task owned by the node and returns it, before _claim runs and without touching attempts. Only 'running' tasks go through _requeue_or_lose.

5. No escape. sweep() at fleet.py:163-165 requeues only when the owning node is offline. Polling keeps last_seen fresh, so the node never goes offline. The task therefore never reaches max_attempts or 'lost', and the node never claims other work.

The same lock-up happens with any task the node cannot decode, so NaN is just one trigger. The reporter's temp-copy run, in which three re-polls returned the same task with attempts still 1, matches this code path.

Medium severity is reasonable. Triggering it needs a token holder, or any malformed or incompatible task, and it blocks a node until someone cancels the task by hand. Before this PR the task was orphaned but the node kept serving other work. | fix: In next_task's re-delivery branch (fleet.py:231-233), count each re-delivery, for example `t.meta['deliveries'] = t.meta.get('deliveries', 0) + 1` followed by save_meta. Once it passes a small cap (for example 3, or max_attempts), call `self._requeue_or_lose(t, 'node repeatedly failed to start task')` and continue to _claim instead of returning t. Separately, reject non-finite numbers at input: use `json.dumps(payload, allow_nan=False)` in create_task (and in federated.py:216), wrapping the ValueError as a 400, and parse request bodies with `parse_constant` that raises. On the Swift side, NodeService.execute should POST /complete with status=failed when the task is undecodable but its id can be recovered, rather than silently returning.

title: PUT artifact rejected before the body is read leaves the unread body on the keep-alive connection, and the next request on it is reset
scenario: A node is uploading adapter.safetensors for a task it no longer owns, for example one cancelled by the new expire() round deadline, cancelled while assigned, or requeued. The upload may also have a bad name or be over the 64 MB cap. put_artifact now raises PermissionError or ValueError before read_body is called. The handler sends 409 or 400 on an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection and leaves Content-Length bytes unread. BaseHTTPRequestHandler then parses the adapter bytes as the next request line, sends an error and closes the socket with data still unread, which causes a TCP RST. The client's next request on that pooled connection, typically POST /tasks/{id}/complete (not idempotent, so URLSession does not retry it), fails with a connection reset instead of a clean 2xx or 409. Over slower links the RST can also arrive before the 409 is read. Before this PR the body was always consumed first (raw_reader() was evaluated before the call), so this desync is new.
evidence: Ran in a temp copy of origin/fix-worker over one http.client keep-alive connection: claim a task, cancel it, PUT 8 MB to /tasks/{id}/artifacts/adapter.safetensors. The PUT returned 409, then the next request on the same connection raised ConnectionResetError(10054). This happened in 3 of 3 runs. fleet.py:282-286 checks ownership and name before `data = read_body(MAX_ARTIFACT)`. jobworker._route never sets close_connection or drains the body on an error.
fix: When rejecting a PUT before reading the body, either set `self.close_connection = True` and send `Connection: close` in the handler, or discard Content-Length bytes in bounded chunks before replying. The simplest change is for _route to mark the connection for close whenever the raw reader was not called on a request that has a body. The ownership-before-buffering protection stays in place.
notes:
UPHELD(high): I could not refute the claim; the code on origin/fix-worker confirms it. The handler uses protocol_version "HTTP/1.1", so connections are keep-alive. In worker/fleet.py, put_artifact calls self._owned() first, which raises PermissionError and is mapped to 409. It then validates the name (ValueError, mapped to 400). Only after both does it reach `data = read_body(MAX_ARTIFACT)`. The router now passes `raw_reader` uncalled. The diff shows the change from `raw_reader()` to `raw_reader`, so before this PR the body was always read before the ownership and name checks. jobworker.Handler._route catches the error, calls self._send(status, body) and returns. It never reads the remaining Content-Length bytes and never sets close_connection. BaseHTTPRequestHandler then reads the unread upload bytes as the next request line. That produces a 400 or 414 error and a close with unread receive data, which gives the RST that the reporter reproduced (ConnectionResetError 10054, 3 of 3 runs).

The over-cap case (Content-Length above the limit) is not new: _raw already raised before reading on integration. The not-owned and bad-name cases are regressions from this PR. Severity is low. The node has lost the task, so the follow-up request would most likely get a 409 anyway, and the damage is a reset connection plus one failed, non-retried request, not lost data. | fix: In jobworker.Handler._route, track whether the raw reader or _body consumed the body. Wrap self._raw in a closure that sets a flag. After the router returns, if the request had Content-Length > 0 and the body was not consumed, set `self.close_connection = True` and send a `Connection: close` header with the response. Alternatively, drain the bytes in bounded chunks, but only for requests from authenticated owners. In put_artifact, keep the ownership and name checks before the read.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute this claim. The code on origin/fix-worker confirms it. In worker/fleet.py, put_artifact calls self._owned(), which raises PermissionError, and then the name check, which raises ValueError. Both run before `data = read_body(MAX_ARTIFACT)`. The diff against integration shows the router changed from passing `raw_reader()`, which read the body before the call, to passing `raw_reader`, which reads it lazily. So the ownership and name rejections now leave the body unread, and they did not before.

In worker/jobworker.py, the Handler uses protocol_version "HTTP/1.1". `_route` turns the router's (409 or 400, ...) result into `_send()`. `_send` writes only Content-Type and Content-Length. It sends no `Connection: close` header, never sets `self.close_connection`, and never drains rfile. Nothing else in the code drains it either. BaseHTTPRequestHandler.handle() then keeps the connection alive and reads the leftover adapter bytes as the next request line. That gives a 400 or 414 and a close while unread data is still buffered, which causes a TCP RST. This matches the reported ConnectionResetError in 3 of 3 runs.

One nuance: the over-cap case (Content-Length > 64 MB) was already undrained before this PR, because `_raw` raised before reading. Only the not-owned and bad-name rejections are new. The low severity fits, since the client usually recovers or the task is already moot, but the next non-idempotent request on the reused connection, such as POST /complete, can fail. | fix: In jobworker Handler._route, or wherever an error response is sent, track whether `_raw` or `_body` consumed the body. If Content-Length > 0 and the body was not read, set `self.close_connection = True` and send a `Connection: close` header before end_headers. A simpler alternative for small bodies is to drain up to some bound and close above it. This also covers the existing over-cap path in `_raw`.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute this. The code and an independent reproduction both confirm it.

Code (origin/fix-worker):
- fleet.py handle(): on integration the route was `fleet.put_artifact(..., raw_reader())`, so the body was always read before any check. The PR changes this to pass `raw_reader`, and put_artifact now calls `self._owned()` (which raises PermissionError -> 409, or LookupError -> 404) and the name check (ValueError -> 400) before `data = read_body(MAX_ARTIFACT)`.
- jobworker.py Handler uses protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1". `_route` sends the error response through `_send` but never drains `Content-Length` bytes and never sets `close_connection`. The unread body then stays on the keep-alive socket and gets parsed as the next request line.

Reproduction: I ran this in a mktemp dir outside the repo, using fleet.py, federated.py and jobworker.py from origin/fix-worker and the same make_router/serve setup as test_fleet.py. Over one http.client keep-alive connection I sent PUT /tasks/t20260101T000000Z-deadbeef/artifacts/adapter.safetensors?node_id=nodeA with 8 MB, and the server answered 404 "no such task". The next request on the same connection, GET /fleet/nodes, raised ConnectionResetError(10054). The claim used the cancelled-task/409 path, and the unknown-task/404 path I used goes through the same pre-read rejection, so the desync applies to every reject-before-read branch.

Pre-existing variants of the same issue, not caused by this PR: the `_auth` 401 path and an oversized Content-Length in `_raw` also reply without draining the body. These are not regressions.

Impact: a node whose task was cancelled or requeued mid-upload can have its follow-up request (for example POST /tasks/{id}/complete) on the pooled connection fail with a reset instead of a clean status. The node already handles failures on this path, so low severity is right. | fix: In jobworker._route, track whether the raw reader was called. If the request had a nonzero Content-Length and the body was never read, set `self.close_connection = True` and send a `Connection: close` header with the error response. The alternative is to drain up to a bounded number of bytes in chunks before replying. Apply the same treatment to the `_auth` 401 path and to `_raw`'s too-large rejection. The ownership check still runs before any buffering.

title: The privacy fixes (403 on per-device adapters, use_local_data opt-in) only cover Federation rounds; a direct POST /tasks train_lora bypasses both
scenario: A token holder sends POST /tasks {"kind":"train_lora","node":"ipad-x","payload":{"base_model":"<model>","use_local_data":true,"iterations":5000,"learning_rate":0.1}}. handle() calls create_task(kind, payload, node) with no round_id and no train_lora payload validation, so the server-side use_local_data opt-in in Federation.start is never applied. If the device allows document training, the iPad trains on its documents and uploads adapter.safetensors. artifact_path returns 403 only when task.meta has a round_id, so GET /tasks/{id}/artifacts/adapter.safetensors serves the raw per-device adapter. The PR body says 'only the averaged adapter is published'.
evidence: fleet.py:303 `if task.meta.get("round_id"): raise Forbidden(...)`. round_id is set only through Federation.start's create_task(..., round_id=rid). The POST /tasks route (fleet.py handle) calls `fleet.create_task(str(b.get("kind", "")), b.get("payload") or {}, b.get("node") or None)` and accepts kind train_lora with any payload.
fix: Either reject kind 'train_lora' on public POST /tasks (only Federation may create it), or apply the Forbidden check to every train_lora task (`if task.meta.get("round_id") or task.meta["kind"] == "train_lora"`) and force payload.use_local_data to False on tasks that did not come from Federation.start.
notes:
UPHELD(high): Checked at origin/fix-worker. Each step of the claimed path holds:
1. worker/fleet.py handle(): POST /tasks calls fleet.create_task(str(b.get("kind","")), b.get("payload") or {}, b.get("node") or None). No round_id is passed.
2. create_task (fleet.py ~173) accepts "train_lora" (it is in TASK_KINDS). It only checks the payload's type and size, the node, and a prompt for "generate". It does nothing to use_local_data.
3. The opt-in logic (use_local = spec.get("use_local_data", False) is True) exists only in worker/federated.py ~202, inside Federation.start. That is also the only caller that sets round_id (create_task(..., round_id=rid), federated.py:229).
4. artifact_path (fleet.py:303) returns 403 only when task.meta.get("round_id") is set. Otherwise it serves any listed artifact.
5. The iPad side (ios/AgentConsole/Node/NodeService.swift runTrain) runs train_lora with roundId optional (it defaults to ""). It adds localSamples() whenever payload.useLocalData is true. I found no further device-side allow check in that function. It then always uploads adapter.safetensors with putArtifact.
So a direct POST /tasks train_lora with use_local_data:true trains on the iPad's imported documents. The resulting per-device adapter can then be downloaded from GET /tasks/{id}/artifacts/adapter.safetensors, outside the Federation privacy guards.

Two things keep this low:
- The caller must already hold the fleet token, the same one that can start Federation rounds.
- A single-node Federation round already makes the "averaged" adapter equal to one device's adapter.
The fix-worker guarantee is still inconsistent with the PR's claim that only the averaged adapter is published. | fix: In fleet.py handle(), reject kind == "train_lora" on public POST /tasks with 400 "train_lora tasks are created by /fed/rounds". Alternatively, add an internal-only flag to create_task that only Federation.start sets. Also make artifact_path deny any task whose meta kind is train_lora, so per-device adapters can never be downloaded. If use_local_data should be device-gated, have NodeService.runTrain check the device's document-training setting before calling localSamples().

UPHELD(high): I confirmed this on origin/fix-worker.

1. Nothing stops a direct train_lora task. The POST /tasks route in worker/fleet.py handle() (about line 370) calls `fleet.create_task(kind, payload, node)` with no round_id. create_task (fleet.py:173) only checks that the kind is in TASK_KINDS = {"generate","train_lora"}, that the payload is a dict, its size, and that the node exists. It validates payload contents only for "generate". So `{"kind":"train_lora","payload":{"base_model":...,"use_local_data":true}}` is queued exactly as sent.

2. The download block depends only on round_id. artifact_path (fleet.py:301-306) raises Forbidden only when `task.meta.get("round_id")` is set. round_id comes in only through Federation's create_task(..., round_id=...) in worker/federated.py. For a direct task the check is skipped, and GET /tasks/{id}/artifacts/adapter.safetensors serves the raw per-device adapter once it has been uploaded. test_fleet.py only checks the 403 for tasks created by a round.

3. The iPad has no setting that blocks document training, so the claim actually understates the problem. In ios/AgentConsole/Node/NodeService.swift, runTrain (around line 379) runs `if p.useLocalData ?? false { samples += await localSamples() }`. localSamples() (line 403) reads every imported document and applies no check. A search for allow/allowDocument settings in ios/ found nothing. The claim's condition "if the device allows document training" is therefore always true. The only requirement is that the payload's base_model matches the model loaded on the iPad.

4. The use_local_data check in federated.py:202 only reads the same caller-supplied flag. It is not a separate consent step, so routing through Federation adds no protection beyond the 403 on artifacts.

Net effect: anyone with a token can bypass the "only the averaged adapter is published" guarantee. They can train on one iPad's imported documents with any iterations and learning rate, then download that device's adapter, which may have memorised those documents. Severity stays low to medium, because a token holder already controls the fleet, but this is a real gap in the privacy property the PR claims to provide. | fix: Treat train_lora as a kind only Federation can create. In handle(), POST /tasks should reject kind "train_lora" with a 400 (or create_task should require round_id for train_lora). artifact_path should also refuse every train_lora artifact, not just round tasks: `if task.meta.get("round_id") or task.meta["kind"] == "train_lora": raise Forbidden(...)`. Separately, add a setting on the iPad (off by default) that NodeService.runTrain checks before calling localSamples(). Right now use_local_data is honoured without the device owner ever opting in.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute the claim. I traced the scenario through the code on origin/fix-worker:
1. In fleet.py handle(), the POST /tasks route (line ~370) calls `fleet.create_task(kind, payload, node)` with no extra fields. kind "train_lora" is in TASK_KINDS. create_task only checks payload contents for "generate", so a train_lora payload goes through with `use_local_data: true` and no round_id.
2. On the iPad, NodeService.swift (fix-node:537-594, and fix-worker:379-385) accepts a train_lora payload whose roundId is missing (`p.roundId ?? ""`). The only document gate is the device's allowDocumentTraining. If that is on, the iPad trains on its documents and uploads the adapter.
3. artifact_path (fleet.py:303) raises Forbidden only when `task.meta.get("round_id")` is set. round_id gets into meta only through the `**extra` argument, which only Federation.start passes (federated.py:229). So GET /tasks/{id}/artifacts/adapter.safetensors returns the raw adapter trained on that one device's documents.
4. PR #4 states that only the averaged adapter is published. This direct route breaks that promise.

One correction to the claim: use_local_data is not really bypassed. The direct caller still has to set it to true explicitly, and the device must still allow document training. What is actually bypassed is the 403 that keeps per-device adapters private. The caller also needs the fleet token, and that token holder could probably run a 1-node federation anyway (min 2 examples per node does not apply when local data is used). That limits the impact, so low severity fits. | fix: In fleet.py handle(), reject kind "train_lora" on the public POST /tasks with a 400 ("train_lora tasks are created via /fed/rounds"), so federated training goes only through Federation. Alternatively, make artifact_path raise Forbidden for any task with `task.meta["kind"] == "train_lora"`, and have Federation serve the per-device adapters it needs straight from disk. Separately, if 1-node rounds with use_local_data are allowed, they would also publish an average that is really one device's adapter. Consider requiring at least 2 contributors when use_local_data is true.
